title: Mini-batch kernel $k$-means
claim: Our mini-batch kernel variants keep clustering quality close to the full-batch method while cutting runtime by orders of magnitude.
layout: 4 dataset panels in a row, shared legend below, dual-axis bars
description: A single row of four grouped bar-chart panels, one per dataset (mnist_784, har, letter, pendigits). Each panel groups bars under ARI, NMI and runtime. Quality scores (ARI, NMI) are on a left linear axis, with error bars. Runtime is on a right log-scale axis in seconds. Six methods are encoded by color and hatching: blue Kernel, teal Truncated β-MiniBatch Kernel, orange β-MiniBatch Kernel and MiniBatch Kernel, and purple β-MiniBatch and MiniBatch. The orange and teal bars (our kernel variants) have similar quality to the blue full-batch Kernel but much shorter runtime bars. Black segments at the bottom of runtime bars mark the time spent computing the kernel. A two-row legend sits below the panels. The eye goes first to the tall blue runtime bars, then to the much shorter bars next to them.
caption: Our results for a batch size of size 1024 and $\tau = 200$ using the Gaussian kernel. We use the $\beta$ prefix to denote the algorithm uses the learning rate of [ref]. Black denotes the time required to compute the kernel.
abstract: We present the first mini-batch kernel $k$-means algorithm, offering an order of magnitude improvement in running time compared to the full batch algorithm. A single iteration of our algorithm takes $\widetilde{O}(kb^2)$ time, significantly faster than the $O(n^2)$ time required by the full batch kernel $k$-means, where $n$ is the dataset size and $b$ is the batch size. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our algorithm consistently achieves a 10-100x speedup with minimal loss in quality, addressing the slow runtime that has limited kernel $k$-means adoption in practice. We further complement these results with a theoretical analysis under an early stopping condition, proving that with a batch size of $\widetildeÎ©(\max \{Î³^{4}, Î³^{2}\} \cdot Îµ^{-2})$, the algorithm terminates in $O(Î³^2/Îµ)$ iterations with high probability, where $Î³$ bounds the norm of points in feature space and $Îµ$ is a termination threshold. Our analysis holds for any reasonable center initialization, and when using $k$-means++ initialization, the algorithm achieves an approximation ratio of $O(\log k)$ in expectation. For normalized kernels, such as Gaussian or Laplacian it holds that $Î³=1$. Taking $Îµ= O(1)$ and $b=Î(\log n)$, the algorithm terminates in $O(1)$ iterations, with each iteration running in $\widetilde{O}(k)$ time.
